screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will have four concrete, demonstrable skills. First, you'll be able to declare functions in Solidity with parameters and returns that make your code modular and testable. That matters because clear function boundaries reduce bugs and make reasoning about state changes possible. Second, you'll be able to choose and apply the correct visibility specifier—public, private, internal or external—so your contract only exposes the surface it must. A common mistake is defaulting to public; we'll show why minimal visibility reduces attack surface. Third, you'll understand view and pure qualifiers and when their off-chain calls are gas-free, which helps you optimize user interactions while avoiding incorrect assumptions about costs. Fourth, you'll confidently use global variables like msg. sender, msg. value and block. timestamp to implement access control, payments, and time-based logic. Each objective includes a small mnemonic to help you remember the rule and a milestone indicating practical competence.

screens.title: Functions: Syntax, Parameters, and Returns
screens.narratorSegment: Functions are the executable building blocks of a smart contract. In Solidity you name a function, define typed parameters, optionally declare return types, and specify qualifiers like visibility and state mutability. A clear function signature acts as a contract between callers and implementation. For example, an add function that takes two unsigned integers and returns their sum communicates intent and ensures type safety. Parameters are typed, so the compiler enforces correct usage and reduces runtime surprises. Returns can be single values or multiple typed values, which makes functions a useful way to compute and hand back results rather than mutating state. In practice, prefer small, single-responsibility functions: they are easier to test and reason about. A common misconception is that every operation must be done inside one large function; instead, break logic into smaller functions and use internal calls where appropriate. Example: imagine a token transfer where you separate balance checks, state updates, and events into three small functions. This reduces mistakes and makes unit testing straightforward. As a takeaway, treat function signatures as part of your contract's public A P I: document parameter meaning, return units, and expected side effects so that callers know whether they will pay gas or only read state. What small helper can you extract from a long function in your codebase?

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.2›Functions
Definition

Function declaration explained

A function has a name, typed inputs, an optional return type, visibility and mutability qualifiers. Use them to communicate intent and constraints.

Explanation bullets
  • Parameters are typed; the compiler enforces types at compile time.
  • Returns can be single or multiple typed values for clearer APIs.
  • Mutability qualifiers like view and pure describe state interaction.
  • Keep functions focused to simplify testing and security reasoning.
Key Takeaway

Design function signatures as your contract's API: typed inputs, explicit returns, and clear mutability make behavior predictable.

Code example
function add(uint256 a, uint256 b) public pure returns (uint256) {
  return a + b;
}
Concrete example

Separate validation, state update and event emission into distinct functions. For instance, validate inputs first, then update balances, then emit an event.

Check your understanding: which part should be pure, and which must be state-modifying?

screens.title: Visibility Specifiers: public vs private vs internal vs external
screens.narratorSegment: Visibility specifiers determine who can call a function or read a state variable. Public is the most permissive: it creates an externally callable function, and when used on a state variable Solidity automatically creates a getter. Private restricts access to only the defining contract; inheriting contracts cannot see private members. Internal is similar to private but allows inheriting contracts to read and call the member, which makes it useful for shared helper logic across a contract family. External applies only to functions and can only be invoked from outside the contract, typically by transactions or other contracts. External functions are more gas-efficient for large calldata arrays because they can read parameters directly from calldata rather than copying to memory. A common misconception is that external functions can be called internally without cost; they cannot be called by ordinary internal calls. If you need to invoke an external function from inside the same contract, you must perform an external call which carries overhead. A practical rule: prefer the least permissive visibility that still supports your intended usage. Example: helper routines used only internally should be private or internal; A P I endpoints should be public or external depending on the data patterns. Understanding these differences reduces accidental exposure of sensitive state and narrows attack surfaces.

keyIdea.text: Choose the minimum visibility that supports required access—private/internal for internal logic, public/external for API functions.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.2›Visibility
Comparison

Who can call or read?

public

Accessible internally, externally, and by inheriting contracts. State variables get an automatic getter.

private

Only visible inside the defining contract. Use for sensitive helpers and internal-only data.

internal

Visible in the contract and by inheritors. Good for shared internal logic across a family of contracts.

external

Callable only from outside the contract. More efficient for large calldata arrays but cannot be invoked by internal calls.

Misconception check: external functions are not interchangeable with public for internal calls. If you try to call an external function as if it were internal, the compiler or runtime will not behave as expected.
Concrete example
uint256 private secretValue;
uint256 public publicValue;
uint256 internal internalValue;
function externalOnly(uint256 x) external pure returns (uint256) { return x * 2; }
Check your understanding

Which visibility prevents inheriting contracts from accessing a state variable? Answer: private. Why? Because only the defining contract has access.

screens.title: Calling External Functions and Gas Efficiency
screens.narratorSegment: External functions are optimized for parameters that come from the transaction's calldata, especially for large arrays. When you mark a function external and accept a large array, the function can read the parameter directly from calldata without copying it into memory, which reduces gas usage on the call. That makes external attractive for bulk-read or bulk-processing APIs. However, external functions cannot be called the same way internally; an internal call to an external function requires an explicit external invocation that costs gas and acts like an external transaction. The process to decide is simple: if a function is part of your contract's external A P I and will receive large calldata blobs, consider external for efficiency. If it's a helper that will be invoked internally or by inheritors, prefer internal or private. A typical pattern is to provide a public wrapper that performs access checks and then calls an internal function that contains the shared implementation. This pattern keeps the efficient external interface while preserving internal reuse. Watch out for a misconception that external always saves gas; for small inputs the difference can be negligible and external internal call patterns can introduce additional overhead. As a takeaway, choose visibility based on call origin and data size.

keyIdea.text: Use external for public APIs that accept large calldata; provide internal implementations for reuse to avoid costly self-calls.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.2›External & Gas
Process Flow

Decide external vs internal

Step 1 — Identify callers

Will the function be called from other contracts or accounts? If yes, external/public is needed.

Step 2 — Inspect data size

Large arrays favor external for calldata efficiency; small arguments may not benefit.

Step 3 — Plan reuse

If internal reuse is required, implement logic in an internal function and expose an external wrapper if needed.

Example pattern
function doWorkExternal(uint256[] calldata items) external {
  require(items.length > 0);
  _doWorkInternal(items);
}
function _doWorkInternal(uint256[] memory items) internal {
  // shared implementation
}
Misconception: calling an external function from inside the same contract by using its name is not allowed; an explicit external call is needed and that adds overhead.

screens.title: view and pure: Read-only vs Stateless
screens.narratorSegment: Solidity provides mutability qualifiers to indicate whether a function interacts with contract state. A view function promises not to modify state — it may read state variables but cannot change them. A pure function promises not to read or write state; it operates purely on input parameters and local variables. This distinction matters for gas and for how you use the function. Calling view or pure functions from off-chain code, for example from a web UI or a script, invokes a local node call that does not create a transaction and therefore costs no gas. But if you call a view or pure function as part of an on-chain transaction, it consumes gas as part of the transaction execution. A common misconception is assuming view always costs no gas; that only holds for off-chain calls. Practically, label functions view or pure whenever possible to express intent and enable gas-free queries from clients. Example: a balance lookup is view; a math helper that computes a result from inputs only should be pure. Using these qualifiers correctly improves clarity, helps auditors, and can save users money when you design careful read paths for UI interactions. What function in your codebase can be converted to view or pure to make its intent clearer?

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.2›view & pure
Definition

Read-only and stateless functions

view

Can read state but must not modify it. Useful for queries like returning balances.

pure

Cannot read or modify state; operates only on inputs. Ideal for math helpers.

Misconception check: view does not imply zero gas in all contexts; only off-chain calls are gas-free. When included inside a transaction, these functions still consume gas as part of execution.
Examples
function getBalance() public view returns (uint256) {
  return balances[msg.sender];
}
function multiply(uint256 a, uint256 b) public pure returns (uint256) {
  return a * b;
}
Pro tip

Prefer pure for deterministic helpers; prefer view for reads. This signals intent to callers and auditors.

screens.title: Global Variables: msg.sender, msg.value, block.timestamp
screens.narratorSegment: Global variables provide the runtime context a contract receives with each call. msg. sender is the calling account's address and is the basis of access control and ownership checks. msg. value is the amount of Wei sent with the call, and it is essential for payable functions that accept Ether. block. timestamp provides the approximate Unix timestamp of the current block and is commonly used for deadlines and time windows. Use these globals to enforce who can call critical functions, to record payments, and to establish time-based conditions. For example, in a SimpleWallet the constructor stores the deployer's address in owner using msg. sender, the deposit function reads msg. value to credit the sender's balance, and withdrawals check msg. sender == owner to guard funds. Be cautious: block. timestamp can be slightly manipulated by miners within a small window, so avoid relying on it for high-precision or security-critical randomness. Another common pitfall is trusting msg. sender in multi-step flows without considering contract calls vs externally owned accounts; sometimes you might need to check the origin of a transaction or use additional checks for contract interactions. As a takeaway, treat these globals as the explicit inputs to your contract's logic and validate them carefully.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.2›Globals
Architecture

Transaction and block context

msg.sender
Who called the function

Use for ownership checks and per-caller state like balances.

msg.value
Amount sent with the call

Essential for payable functions and recording deposits.

block.timestamp
When the block was mined

Use for deadlines and vesting. Remember potential minor miner manipulation.

Concrete wallet snippet
constructor() {
  owner = msg.sender; // deployer becomes owner
}
function deposit() public payable {
  require(msg.value > 0, "Deposit must be > 0");
  balances[msg.sender] += msg.value;
}
Misconception check: block.timestamp should not be used for secure randomness. Small shifts can be introduced by miners so avoid relying on it for critical entropy.

screens.title: SimpleWallet: deposit and withdraw flow
screens.narratorSegment: Let's step through the SimpleWallet contract to see how these concepts work together. The constructor sets owner equal to msg. sender at deploy time, establishing the deployer as the controlling account. The deposit function is marked payable so it can receive Ether; inside it require(msg. value > 0) ensures callers send a positive amount, and balances[msg. sender] is incremented by msg. value, recording who sent how much. This uses msg. sender to attribute funds correctly and msg. value to measure the amount. The withdrawAll function enforces access control with require(msg. sender == owner), ensuring only the owner can drain the contract. It then reads address(this). balance to compute the contract's total funds, checks that there is something to withdraw, and performs a low-level call to send Ether to the owner. Importantly, the code checks the boolean success return and reverts if the transfer failed. A common mistake is omitting this success check; doing so can silently lose funds or leave the contract in an inconsistent state. As you walk through these lines in Remix, observe transaction logs, events and reverted messages. How does checking success make the difference in failure scenarios?

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.2›SimpleWallet Walkthrough
Code

Key functions

constructor() { owner = msg.sender; }

function deposit() public payable {
  require(msg.value > 0, "Deposit amount must be greater than zero");
  balances[msg.sender] += msg.value;
  emit Deposit(msg.sender, msg.value, block.timestamp);
}

function withdrawAll() public {
  require(msg.sender == owner, "Only the owner can withdraw");
  uint256 amountToWithdraw = address(this).balance;
  (bool success, ) = payable(owner).call{value: amountToWithdraw}("");
  require(success, "Withdrawal failed");
}
Explanation bullets
  • Constructor assigns owner via msg.sender — the deployer becomes the owner.
  • deposit is payable and updates balances[msg.sender] using msg.value.
  • withdrawAll restricts access and checks the low-level call success to avoid silent failures.
Key Takeaway

Always validate msg.value, attribute funds to msg.sender, and check transfer success to avoid lost funds.

screens.title: Common Pitfalls: defaulting to public and unchecked transfers
screens.narratorSegment: Two common mistakes repeatedly cause security issues: making functions and variables more public than necessary, and failing to check the result of external calls when transferring Ether. Defaulting to public or leaving state variables implicitly exposed creates larger attack surfaces and surprising getters. For example, public state variables create automatic getters; if that data is sensitive you should mark it private or internal. The second mistake is omitting the boolean success check when using low-level calls to transfer Ether. A low-level call can fail for many reasons — gas stipend differences, a receiver reverting, or other runtime conditions. If you ignore the success return, your code may continue as if the transfer succeeded, leading to inconsistent state and fund loss. Always require the success boolean or use safe transfer helpers that bubble errors. Another subtle pitfall is trusting block. timestamp for precise timing; because miners can shift it slightly, avoid using it for high-precision timing or randomness. The practical defense is to adopt least-privilege visibility, validate all transfers, and document assumptions in the contract. These small checks are inexpensive and preserve safety.

Public by default and unchecked calls

screens.title: Access Control Patterns: onlyOwner and internal helpers
screens.narratorSegment: A common and robust access control pattern is to implement a public or external function that performs permission checks and then delegate the core logic to an internal function. This lets you keep a clear external A P I while avoiding duplicate code for internal reuse. For example, an onlyOwner check on withdraw would ensure only the contract owner can invoke it, while the actual fund transfer logic lives in a private or internal function that could also be called by derived contracts if needed. This separation improves readability, makes auditing easier, and reduces the chance of accidentally exposing privileged logic. Another pattern is to mark sensitive state variables private while exposing controlled getters, which prevents accidental writes or direct access from inheritors. Misconceptions arise when developers conflate inheritance visibility: private prevents inheritors from accessing data, internal permits it. As a rule, encapsulate privileged operations behind explicit permission checks and funnel shared implementation into internal helpers so you can maintain least-privilege exposure without duplicating code. Access Control Patterns: onlyOwner and internal helpers means use permissioned external/public functions as guards, and delegate implementation to internal/private helpers for reuse and safety.. In practical terms, combine owner checks with internal implementations for clear apis. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4›Chapter 4.2›Access Control
Design Pattern

Guard then delegate

  • Public/external entrypoint performs require(msg.sender == owner) or similar role checks.
  • Internal/private function contains the actual state changes and can be reused by inheritors.
  • Keep privileged state private when possible and expose controlled getters if needed.
Misconception: making everything internal is not a substitute for explicit permission checks on public APIs. Both patterns are complementary.
Pattern snippet
function withdrawAll() public {
  require(msg.sender == owner, 'Only owner');
  _withdrawInternal();
}
function _withdrawInternal() internal {
  // transfer logic and checks
}
Key Takeaway

Separate permission checks from implementation to make audits and reuse straightforward.

screens.title: Remember These Practical Rules
screens.narratorSegment: Before you close this lesson, keep three practical rules in your toolkit. Rule one: default to the least permissive visibility and only expose what you must. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will make functions the center of your smart contract design. You will learn how to declare functions with parameters and return values, and why visibility specifiers are a security-critical choice. We'll contrast public, private, internal and external to show how they limit or permit calls from accounts, from other contracts, and from inheriting contracts. You'll also learn the operational difference between view and pure functions and why calling them off-chain can be gas-free. Finally, we'll look at three global variables — msg. sender, msg. value and block. timestamp — that provide transaction and block context and are the building blocks for access control, payments, and time-based logic. As a concrete example, we'll step through a simple wallet that accepts deposits and restricts withdrawals to the deployer. Throughout, I'll point out common mistakes such as defaulting to public visibility and forgetting to check the success of a low-level transfer. By the end you'll understand not just the syntax, but the practical trade-offs that affect cost, safety, and reusability in real contracts. Ready to see how functions control behavior and exposure? Let's explore the key topics that follow.

By the end of this chapter you will have four concrete, demonstrable skills. First, you'll be able to declare functions in Solidity with parameters and returns that make your code modular and testable. That matters because clear function boundaries reduce bugs and make reasoning about state changes possible. Second, you'll be able to choose and apply the correct visibility specifier—public, private, internal or external—so your contract only exposes the surface it must. A common mistake is defaulting to public; we'll show why minimal visibility reduces attack surface. Third, you'll understand view and pure qualifiers and when their off-chain calls are gas-free, which helps you optimize user interactions while avoiding incorrect assumptions about costs. Fourth, you'll confidently use global variables like msg. sender, msg. value and block. timestamp to implement access control, payments, and time-based logic. Each objective includes a small mnemonic to help you remember the rule and a milestone indicating practical competence.

This second objectives screen maps each learning goal to a small practice and a verification check. For functions, you'll declare a function with two inputs and a typed return, then write a unit-style check that validates its result. For visibility, you'll change a function to private, deploy a demo contract, and observe compilation errors when you attempt an external call — that demonstrates access control in action. For view and pure, you'll perform an off-chain call in Remix to observe no gas consumption, and then wrap the same call inside a transaction to see the cost difference. For the global variables objective, you'll deploy the SimpleWallet, make a deposit that sends Ether, and attempt a withdrawal from a non-owner account to verify that require(msg. sender == owner) reverts. Each practice is short, repeatable, and directly tied to the competency milestone so you can prove the skill.

Functions are the executable building blocks of a smart contract. In Solidity you name a function, define typed parameters, optionally declare return types, and specify qualifiers like visibility and state mutability. A clear function signature acts as a contract between callers and implementation. For example, an add function that takes two unsigned integers and returns their sum communicates intent and ensures type safety. Parameters are typed, so the compiler enforces correct usage and reduces runtime surprises. Returns can be single values or multiple typed values, which makes functions a useful way to compute and hand back results rather than mutating state. In practice, prefer small, single-responsibility functions: they are easier to test and reason about. A common misconception is that every operation must be done inside one large function; instead, break logic into smaller functions and use internal calls where appropriate. Example: imagine a token transfer where you separate balance checks, state updates, and events into three small functions. This reduces mistakes and makes unit testing straightforward. As a takeaway, treat function signatures as part of your contract's public A P I: document parameter meaning, return units, and expected side effects so that callers know whether they will pay gas or only read state. What small helper can you extract from a long function in your codebase?

Visibility specifiers determine who can call a function or read a state variable. Public is the most permissive: it creates an externally callable function, and when used on a state variable Solidity automatically creates a getter. Private restricts access to only the defining contract; inheriting contracts cannot see private members. Internal is similar to private but allows inheriting contracts to read and call the member, which makes it useful for shared helper logic across a contract family. External applies only to functions and can only be invoked from outside the contract, typically by transactions or other contracts. External functions are more gas-efficient for large calldata arrays because they can read parameters directly from calldata rather than copying to memory. A common misconception is that external functions can be called internally without cost; they cannot be called by ordinary internal calls. If you need to invoke an external function from inside the same contract, you must perform an external call which carries overhead. A practical rule: prefer the least permissive visibility that still supports your intended usage. Example: helper routines used only internally should be private or internal; A P I endpoints should be public or external depending on the data patterns. Understanding these differences reduces accidental exposure of sensitive state and narrows attack surfaces.

External functions are optimized for parameters that come from the transaction's calldata, especially for large arrays. When you mark a function external and accept a large array, the function can read the parameter directly from calldata without copying it into memory, which reduces gas usage on the call. That makes external attractive for bulk-read or bulk-processing APIs. However, external functions cannot be called the same way internally; an internal call to an external function requires an explicit external invocation that costs gas and acts like an external transaction. The process to decide is simple: if a function is part of your contract's external A P I and will receive large calldata blobs, consider external for efficiency. If it's a helper that will be invoked internally or by inheritors, prefer internal or private. A typical pattern is to provide a public wrapper that performs access checks and then calls an internal function that contains the shared implementation. This pattern keeps the efficient external interface while preserving internal reuse. Watch out for a misconception that external always saves gas; for small inputs the difference can be negligible and external internal call patterns can introduce additional overhead. As a takeaway, choose visibility based on call origin and data size.

Solidity provides mutability qualifiers to indicate whether a function interacts with contract state. A view function promises not to modify state — it may read state variables but cannot change them. A pure function promises not to read or write state; it operates purely on input parameters and local variables. This distinction matters for gas and for how you use the function. Calling view or pure functions from off-chain code, for example from a web UI or a script, invokes a local node call that does not create a transaction and therefore costs no gas. But if you call a view or pure function as part of an on-chain transaction, it consumes gas as part of the transaction execution. A common misconception is assuming view always costs no gas; that only holds for off-chain calls. Practically, label functions view or pure whenever possible to express intent and enable gas-free queries from clients. Example: a balance lookup is view; a math helper that computes a result from inputs only should be pure. Using these qualifiers correctly improves clarity, helps auditors, and can save users money when you design careful read paths for UI interactions. What function in your codebase can be converted to view or pure to make its intent clearer?

Global variables provide the runtime context a contract receives with each call. msg. sender is the calling account's address and is the basis of access control and ownership checks. msg. value is the amount of Wei sent with the call, and it is essential for payable functions that accept Ether. block. timestamp provides the approximate Unix timestamp of the current block and is commonly used for deadlines and time windows. Use these globals to enforce who can call critical functions, to record payments, and to establish time-based conditions. For example, in a SimpleWallet the constructor stores the deployer's address in owner using msg. sender, the deposit function reads msg. value to credit the sender's balance, and withdrawals check msg. sender == owner to guard funds. Be cautious: block. timestamp can be slightly manipulated by miners within a small window, so avoid relying on it for high-precision or security-critical randomness. Another common pitfall is trusting msg. sender in multi-step flows without considering contract calls vs externally owned accounts; sometimes you might need to check the origin of a transaction or use additional checks for contract interactions. As a takeaway, treat these globals as the explicit inputs to your contract's logic and validate them carefully.

Let's step through the SimpleWallet contract to see how these concepts work together. The constructor sets owner equal to msg. sender at deploy time, establishing the deployer as the controlling account. The deposit function is marked payable so it can receive Ether; inside it require(msg. value > 0) ensures callers send a positive amount, and balances[msg. sender] is incremented by msg. value, recording who sent how much. This uses msg. sender to attribute funds correctly and msg. value to measure the amount. The withdrawAll function enforces access control with require(msg. sender == owner), ensuring only the owner can drain the contract. It then reads address(this). balance to compute the contract's total funds, checks that there is something to withdraw, and performs a low-level call to send Ether to the owner. Importantly, the code checks the boolean success return and reverts if the transfer failed. A common mistake is omitting this success check; doing so can silently lose funds or leave the contract in an inconsistent state.
